title: MPSC Order — Case No. U-20894: Grants in part, and denies in part, the motion for rehearing, reconsideration, and clarification filed by DTE Michigan Lateral Company
text:
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

BEFORE THE MICHIGAN PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION 

* * * * * 

In the matter of the application of
) 
DTE MICHIGAN LATERAL COMPANY 
) 
for issuance of a certificate of public convenience 
)
Case No. U-20894 
and necessity to convert and operate portions of its 
) 
pipeline system and to construct and operate portions ) 
of a pipeline system to provide an additional supply 
) 
source to the areas of Manistee, Traverse City, 
) 
Alpena, and Rogers City. 
) 
) 

At the November 4, 2021 meeting of the Michigan Public Service Commission in Lansing, 
Michigan. 

PRESENT: Hon. Daniel C. Scripps, Chair 

Hon. Tremaine L. Phillips, Commissioner 

Hon. Katherine L. Peretick, Commissioner 

ORDER 

History of Proceedings 

On July 27, 2021, the Commission issued an order in this case (July 27 order) granting, with 
modifications and on partial condition, DTE Michigan Lateral Company’s (DMLC’s) application 
for a certificate of public convenience and necessity relating to its Wet Header System and the 
provision of dry gas transmission service to be provided by DTE Gas Company (DTE Gas) in the 
areas of Traverse City, Alpena, Rogers City, and Manistee. 

On August 26, 2021, DMLC filed a motion for rehearing, reconsideration, and clarification 
(petition for rehearing). On September 15 and 16, 2021, North Bay Energy, LLC (North Bay); 
Riverside Energy Michigan, LLC (Riverside); the Michigan Department of Attorney General 

Page 2 
U-20894 
(Attorney General); and the Commission Staff (Staff) each filed an answer1 to the petition for 
rehearing. 

Petition for Rehearing and Answers 

DMLC files its petition for rehearing to correct ambiguities and to prevent potential 
unintended consequences of the July 27 order and addresses four issues concerning construction 
timing, depth of cover, and contingency costs, to which North Bay, Riverside, the Attorney 
General, and the Staff respond, either in full or in part. 
1. Transition Deadline Due to New Facts and Circumstances Learned After Record Closed 

DMLC states that it has learned new information from its customer (DTE Gas) indicating that 
uncertainty regarding the Wet Header transition due to the July 27 order “may force DTE Gas to 
construct its own new supply line because Federal regulations require DTE Gas to undertake a 
smart pig inspection in 2024 and that cannot be done without an additional Kalkaska to Traverse 
City supply pipeline in place, currently expected to be DMLC’s converted system.” DMLC’s 
petition for rehearing, p. 2; see also, id., pp. 4-5. Considering necessary lead time for construction, 
and absent a transition deadline, which was “anticipated,” so DMLC and DTE Gas “were assured 
the pipeline changeover would occur” in time, DMLC states that DTE Gas “will need to 
immediately commence construct[ion]-related preparation work for that alternative project in order 
to ensure that pipeline is in place by 2024.” Id., pp. 2, 5. DMLC relays this as necessary to allow 
the Wet Header Pipeline to be used for primary service when DTE Gas’s Traverse City pipeline is 
offline for the smart pig inspection required by the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline 

1 In accordance with Mich Admin Code, R 792.10437 (Rule 437), these responsive filings are 
all referred to as “answers.” Rule 437(2). 

Page 3 
U-20894 
and Hazardous Material Safety Administration’s (PHMSA’s) regulations in 2024. Given this 
“PHMSA inspection requirement that the parties did not contemplate during this case and the 
burden and potential duplicative pipelines resulting from the uncertainty of not having a date 
certain for transitioning the Wet Header Pipeline,” DMLC requests that the Commission establish 
a deadline for the conversion of the Wet Header Pipeline in the second quarter of 2022. Id., p. 5. 

North Bay contends that DMLC’s petition for rehearing should be denied, in that it is “nothing 
more than a thinly veiled attempt to re-litigate matters that were fully considered and addressed by 
the Commission in the [July 27] Order.” North Bay’s answer, p. 1. North Bay asserts that 
DMLC’s claims of newly discovered evidence are derived from an affidavit comprised of hearsay 
statements that, “even if considered, do not constitute newly discovered evidence justifying 
rehearing” and that there are “no ambiguities or unintended consequences that were not considered 
by the Commission in its original Order.” Id. 

In more detail, North Bay states that DMLC’s primary request for a back-end date for 
conversion here was an issue that was fully litigated by the parties, considered by the Commission, 
and expressly rejected in the July 27 order. North Bay provides further argument about hearsay 
and the statements contained in the affidavit attached to DMLC’s petition for rehearing, which 
North Bay reasserts the Commission should not consider but, even if considered, are not based on 
newly discovered evidence justifying rehearing. According to North Bay: 
There is no allegation that the PHMSA regulations were amended in any material 
way between when the record was closed in this case and when the Motion for 
Hearing was filed. Upon information and belief, those regulations were not 
amended in that period. If the PHMSA regulations were relevant to this 
proceeding, DMLC could have, and should have, argued that point in its 
evidentiary presentation in this case prior to entry of the Commission’s Order. 

North Bay’s answer, pp. 3-4. North Bay questions why the affidavit claims this is a new fact or 
circumstance, particularly when it and Riverside presented direct testimony, reiterated in briefing, 

Page 4 
U-20894 
that the Commission should not set a back-end date for conversion and should instead defer any 
authorization for conversion until Lambda Gathering LLC’s (Lambda’s) alternate system was 
approved, constructed, and available for service. North Bay asserts that, although DMLC and 
DTE Gas may have anticipated that the Commission would set a back-end date, this was a 
contested issue in the case, and, thus, “[i]f DMLC wished to present evidence related to the 
PHMSA regulations in support of its argument that a back-end date should be provided, DMLC 
was required to present that evidence as a part of its case prior to entry of the Commission Order” 
and “cannot reopen the record to present such evidence now.” Id., pp. 4-5. North Bay adds that 
the statements in the affidavit are not factually accurate, particularly with regard the Traverse City 
pipeline needing to be offline during the smart pig inspection. North Bay “believes that smart pig 
inspections can be conducted with gas flowing in the line, and indeed, that it would be more 
expensive to take a line out of service rather than running the inspection while online.” Id., p. 5, 
n. 2. If the Commission takes the affidavit into consideration, North Bay requests that the parties 
“be given a fair opportunity to investigate the claims in the affidavit and submit competing 
testimony.” Id. 

Riverside asserts that, following extensive briefing, the Commission correctly ruled that 
DMLC’s conversion of the Wet Header System be contingent upon Lambda’s conversion and 
operation of the Lambda Gathering Wet Header System (LGWH) (being the subject of Case 
No. U-21091). Riverside further asserts that DMLC’s petition for rehearing is an attempt to 
relitigate this issue, with DMLC’s request here being “the same position DMLC has taken before – 
that this Commission set a firm deadline in the second quarter of 2022 by which it may convert the 
existing wet header system without regard as to whether the LGWH system is in place.” 
Riverside’s answer, p. 2. Per Riverside, DMLC has not met its burden that the July 27 order was 

Page 5 
U-20894 
incorrect due to proclaimed unintended consequences concerning the conversion, and, thus, 
DMLC’s petition for rehearing must be denied as it relates to this issue. 

Riverside argues that DMLC’s claim here is without support, as DMLC failed to provide a 
citation to, or a clear explanation of, the PHMSA regulation referenced to support its argument 
that a smart pig inspection of its pipeline is required during the timeframe asserted or how the 
purposed inspection would require construction of an entirely new pipeline system just for the 
inspection to be performed. At the very least, according to Riverside, “DMLC’s concerns are 
premature given that Lambda has been granted the approval to construct the LGWH system.” 
Riverside’s answer, p. 4. Riverside states that the September 9, 2021 order in Case No. U-21091 
(September 9 order) granted such approval and “specifically references that Lambda has an 
anticipated in-service date of no later than May of 2022,” recalls the need for seamless 
coordination between the two wet header projects, and found that the LGWH project, when 
constructed and in operation, will serve the convenience and necessity of the public. Riverside’s 
answer, pp. 4-5; September 9 order, p. 2. Given this, Riverside argues that the Commission 
“should not establish a firm date for the transition of the Wet Header System that is not contingent 
upon the completion of the LGWH” as doing so “would effectively nullify the Commissions’ [sic] 
findings, would completely gut the Commission’s [July 27] Order, and would instead create 
uncertainty for all of those producers who rely upon the Wet Header System to transport their gas 
to market.” Id., p. 5. 

The Attorney General also asserts that DMLC is simply seeking to relitigate this issue, with 
DMLC essentially arguing the same position that it took during the case. The Attorney General 
argues that DMLC’s request here, with concern over an inspection three years away and two years 
past when Lambda’s system is expected to be operational, is not newly discovered evidence or 

Page 6 
U-20894 
facts or circumstances arising after the record closed, such that rehearing or any reconsideration is 
warranted. The Attorney General states: 
This is information that DTE Gas clearly knew during the pendency of this 
litigation, which was not brought forth while the record was open. The fact that 
DMLC and DTE Gas are affiliates makes it even more unclear why this would not 
have been communicated or why DMLC would not have known this if it was truly 
relevant to the case. As pointed out in the [Attorney General]’s brief, DMLC 
actually has zero employees, instead contracting with DTE Gas to operate and 
maintain the wet header system. Therefore, DMLC is in essence claiming that it 
did not tell itself about this 2024 inspection. As such, this contention should be 
dismissed out of hand by the Commission. 

Attorney General’s answer, p. 4 (footnote omitted). The Attorney General avers that DMLC’s 
attempt is for another bite at the apple and argues that just because “what DMLC and DTE Gas 
‘anticipated’ the Commission would do did not come to fruition is not a valid rationale for 
rehearing or reconsideration. Additionally, it is not clear what is meant by ‘they were 
assured . . . .’” Id., p. 5. Here, the Attorney General questions “who or what entity assured 
DMLC or DTE Gas of anything or what that statement even means in the context of this part of 
DMLC’s motion.” Id. (emphasis in original); DMLC’s petition for rehearing, p. 5. The Attorney 
General states that this issue was fully addressed in the contested case proceeding and asserts that 
DMLC’s new facts and circumstances are new only because it failed to raise them earlier. Per the 
Attorney General, this does not rise to the level of warranting a rehearing or reconsideration and 
should be rejected. 

The Staff asserts that there is no need for the Commission to provide a deadline. The Staff 
recalls the July 27 order and the discussion therein about representations made relative to May 1, 
2022. The Staff also notes that May 1, 2022, contemplated as the conversion date, is in the middle 
of the second quarter of 2022 and prior to the end of the quarter, being June 30, 2022. The Staff 

Page 7 
U-20894 
also highlights that 2024, for inspection of the Traverse City pipeline, is a 12-month period. The 
Staff states: 
There is no indication in DMLC’s filing that the inspection must occur in the early 
part of the year as opposed to the latter part of the year. Staff finds it strains belief 
that in the two-year period between May 1, 2022, and, say, May 1, 2024, that 
Lambda Energy could not get its pipeline constructed and in operation. Because 
there is such a long-time frame between the expected conversion of the wet header 
system to dry gas transmission and the scheduled inspection of the Traverse City 
pipeline and the need to maintain the wet header system to provide shippers a 
means to get their gas from the wells to the Kalkaska plant, Staff does not 
recommend that the Commission issue a strict deadline for the conversion to occur. 

Staff’s answer, p. 5.2 
2. Ambiguity Regarding Timing of Construction 

DMLC believes that the Commission “intended to authorize DMLC to undertake all 
construction contemplated in the application except for the final conversion of the Wet Header 
Pipeline” but asks for the Commission to confirm this understanding. DMLC’s petition for 
rehearing, p. 2; see also, id., pp. 5-6. Relatedly, DMLC also requests an explanation for how it 
“can request a different approach from the Commission if the Lambda pipeline becomes 
significantly or indefinitely delayed for a small part of the project.” Id., p. 2. DMLC asserts that 
“[t]he Commission’s decision has created an unintended consequence because DMLC must either 
commence construction authorized to proceed and risk that the Lambda Pipeline never comes to 
fruition or wait until the Lambda Pipeline is complete, potentially resulting in a significant delay to 
place the re-purposed pipeline in service.” Id., p. 3. By not setting an end date for the transition, 
DMLC avers that the Commission may unintentionally cause the project in this case to cease. 
DMLC states that its: 

2 The Staff’s answer is not paginated; thus, page 1 starts in natural order with the first page of 
the filing, given no preceding cover pages. 

Page 8 
U-20894 
dilemma is that, if it proceeds with construction now and the Lambda Pipeline is 
delayed or never comes to fruition, DMLC would have assets sitting fallow 
indefinitely (or forever) because the [July 27] Order would never allow DMLC to 
proceed with transitioning the Wet Header Pipeline. To resolve those potential 
ambiguities in light of the Commission’s conclusion that the transition is in the 
public interest, DMLC asks the Commission to establish a deadline in the second 
quarter of 2022 by which, if the Lambda Pipeline is not complete, DMLC could 
commence the Wet Header Pipeline transition. DMLC further requests that the 
Commission authorize DMLC to transition sections of the Wet Header Pipeline as 
those sections are completed rather than delaying the [sic] any portion of the 
transition from occuring [sic] until the entire Lambda pipeline is complete. With a 
date certain in place, DMLC will commit to undertake all of the greenfield work 
that is necessary to quickly complete the transition in order to ensure that the public 
interest to be filled by the Wet Header Pipeline transition is met as soon as possible. 

Id., p. 6. DMLC requests that the Commission clarify these ambiguities to provide it with 
guidance on how to proceed. 

North Bay disagrees with DMLC and argues that DMLC “mischaracterizes the Commission’s 
Order as creating some ambiguity or unintended consequence based on an alleged ‘dilemma’” that 
DMLC now has with moving forward. North Bay’s answer, p. 5. North Bay asserts that this 
dilemma argument is “materially identical” to arguments DMLC made during briefing. Id. (citing 
DMLC’s reply brief, p. 5). Per North Bay, there is no ambiguity in the Commission’s finding that 
“‘the conversion of this critical system must unequivocally be conditioned on Lambda’s 
alternative natural gas gathering system being approved and completed, with, however, the 
Commission’s expectation that diligent and good faith efforts be made by all involved to effectuate 
these projects in a time [sic] manner.’” North Bay’s answer, pp. 5-6 (emphasis in original) (citing 
July 27 order, p. 16). Concluding, North Bay argues that the Commission should reject DMLC’s 
“thinly veiled attempt to disguise the true purpose of its motion – that is, to simply reargue claims 

Page 9 
U-20894 
that were presented by DMLC prior to entry of the Commission’s Order, and that were fully 
considered and rejected by the Commission.” North Bay’s answer, p. 6.3 

The Attorney General contends that DMLC’s request is confusing and does not warrant 
rehearing or reconsideration. The Attorney General states that DMLC appears to be 
arguing/requesting two separate things here, with DMLC first requesting clarification on whether 
it can undertake other construction and conversion related to the Wet Header, provided DMLC 
waits until Lambda’s pipeline is complete before conversion of the Wet Header. To the extent 
there is any ambiguity on this, the Attorney General contends that clarification from the 
Commission may be warranted. However, per the Attorney General, DMLC’s second request in 
this section—to set a transition deadline in the second quarter of 2022—is basically the same 
argument as set forth in point one, “dressed up slightly differently, and similarly seeks to relitigate 
something the Commission decided in its order.” Attorney General’s answer, p. 7. As described 
by the Attorney General: 
DMLC’s motion confusingly bounces back and forth between a request for 
clarification and a request that the Commission simply change its order outright, 
with little to no application in either case to the standard for rehearing. Regardless, 
as noted above, the Commission considered this issue at length and found that the 
most prudent and reasonable path is to ensure that Lambda’s system is completed 
before DMLC transitions the Wet Header. In the extremely unlikely case that 
Lambda’s pipeline is delayed indefinitely, DMLC can come back before the 
Commission at that time for other relief. 

Id., pp. 7-8. 

The Staff agrees with DMLC that the July 27 order allows DMLC “to begin construction of 
the Rogers City Connector [RCC] and the Norwalk Manistee Connector [NMC] pipelines and 

3 North Bay also disputes that any other arguments made by DMLC relative to depth of cover 
and contingency costs support rehearing or any other relief but “defers to the Commission and to 
other parties with a more direct interest in those issues, including the [Commission] Staff and the 
Attorney General.” North Bay’s answer, p. 6, n. 3. 

Page 10 
U-20894 
other construction necessary for the conversion of the wet header pipeline with the final 
conversion to be completed after Lambda has finished with its construction.” Staff’s answer, p. 5. 
Per the Staff, DMLC’s date certain/indefinite delay argument, however, was already raised by 
DMLC and addressed by the Commission, with the Commission detailing the various parties’ 
arguments regarding the timing of the conversion. Id., p. 6 (citing DMLC’s reply brief, pp. 2-5 
and the July 27 order, p. 16). The Staff avers: 
Because this issue has been raised previously and argued, this issue does not fall 
under the heading of newly discovered evidence in Rule 438 [sic: 437]. Further, 
DMLC has not asserted a clear error of law or fact which is the other situation 
contemplated in Rule 438 [sic]. Rehearing’s [sic] are to be granted for good cause, 
as contemplated in the wording of Rule 438 [sic]. The rule takes into account 
changed circumstances not contemplated by the parties and the possibility of error. 
Because DMLC does not meet either of these circumstances provided by the 
Commission’s rule on rehearing’s [sic], Staff recommends that other than clarifying 
that DMLC may begin work as soon as permits and easements are acquired, the 
Commission deny DMLC’s request on this issue. 

Staff’s answer, pp. 6-7. 
3. Depth of Cover 

DMLC requests that the Commission set a uniform depth of coverage of four feet along the 
entire route of the proposed NMC and RCC pipelines, as opposed to alternating depths of five feet 
for agricultural fields and three feet for the remainder. Although DMLC challenges the 
Commission cases cited in support of the Commission’s decision in the July 27 order and also 
“disagrees that the Commission can mandate depths beyond the minimums set by the Gas Safety 
Code barring significant evidence supporting such requirement,” DMLC nevertheless proposes 
this alternative uniform four-foot depth requirement instead, for consistency with Commission 
precedent and to create “better operational characteristics than having a pipeline of differing 
depths.” DMLC’s petition for rehearing, p. 7. 

Page 11 
U-20894 

The Attorney General argues that DMLC’s request here should be denied. The Attorney 
General states that DMLC “cites no error, new evidence, facts, or circumstances, or any 
unintended consequence, and provides no analysis or application to the standard for rehearing or 
reconsideration.” Attorney General’s answer, p. 8. Per the Attorney General, this request is 
simply a new proposal that no other parties have had the chance to examine, which DMLC asks 
the Commission to adopt outside the contested case framework. The Attorney General states that 
the Commission was clear in its decision in the July 27 order, citing the Staff’s concerns over 
agricultural disruptions and accidental strikes, along with other Act 9 cases of late exceeding 
minimum depth of cover standards. According to the Attorney General, “DMLC’s motion does 
not even attempt to raise a basis for rehearing and therefore, the Commission should reject 
DMLC’s request that the Commission order four feet depth of cover along the entire route.” 
Attorney General’s answer, p. 9. 

The Staff disagrees with DMLC and states that the Commission thoroughly reviewed all 
arguments made by DMLC and the Staff on this issue. The Staff reiterates that rehearing is to be 
granted for good cause shown, “not for caprice or on a whim,” and may be granted in the event of 
unforeseen circumstances or in cases of errors of fact or law. Staff’s answer, p. 7. Per the Staff, 
neither of these circumstances have been met with regard to this issue. The Staff states that “[t]he 
Commission’s order clearly lays out the arguments of both Staff and DMLC before stating the 
Commission’s holding,” with the Staff asserting that “DMLC neither brings up an error of fact and 
law or states unforeseen circumstances that would require the Commission to amend its order.” 
Id., p. 8. As such, the Staff recommends that DMLC’s request here be denied. 

Page 12 
U-20894 
4. Contingency Costs 

To address ambiguity, DMLC seeks confirmation that it does not need to undertake a full rate 
case for the contingency costs contemplated in the July 27 order and that it “may instead submit a 
‘completion report’ for the Commission Staff to audit that reflects the amounts DMLC actually 
incurred and uses the same methodology and model Commission Staff reviewed in this case.” 
DMLC’s petition for rehearing, p. 3. More fully: 
DMLC seeks clarification with regard to how it obtains Commission approval for 
contingency costs once DMLC incurs those costs. It is unclear whether the 
Commission would otherwise require DMLC and the other parties to undertake a 
full rate case for contingency costs that were contemplated in this case, so DMLC 
proposes [to] clarify this matter by adopting an alternative approach whereby 
DMLC would submit to the Commission a “completion report” at the conclusion of 
the project reflecting the amounts DMLC actually incurred. DMLC would be 
required to use the same methodology and model that Staff evaluated in this case 
and would be subject to an audit by Staff. Given that the Commission has already 
reviewed the costs reflected in adjusted rates (excluding contingency costs) for 
reasonableness and prudence, it is appropriate for the scope of a future proceeding 
to be limited to considering the reasonableness and prudence of actual costs 
incurred that exceed the currently approved costs. In any event, DMLC asks the 
Commission to clarify its desired process to address contingency costs to ensure 
DMLC follows that process. 

Id., p. 8. 

The Attorney General contends that, similar to its second issue above, DMLC is “again 
confusingly combining a request for clarification with a request that the Commission simply 
approve a new proposal that was not raised in the contested case hearing.” Attorney General’s 
answer, p. 9. In this section, the Attorney General argues that DMLC, again, “raises no error, new 
evidence, facts, or circumstances, or any unintended consequence upon which a rehearing or 
reconsideration might be granted.” Id., p. 10. Similar to above, the Attorney General asserts that 
DMLC has simply come up with a new proposal that no other parties have had the chance to 
examine, asking the Commission, again, for adoption of a proposal outside the contested case 

Page 13 
U-20894 
framework, thus precluding the parties from reviewing actual incurred costs for reasonableness 
and prudence.4 The Attorney General states that the July 27 order provides numerous ways that 
DMLC can seek to recover actual incurred costs, that the Commission was clear in its decision, 
and that DMLC does not attempt to raise a basis for rehearing. The Attorney General thus argues 
that the Commission should reject DMLC’s request. 

The Staff agrees with DMLC’s proposed approach and recommends that DMLC’s request for 
clarification here be granted. The Staff states: 
Under MCL 483.110, the Commission can set rates for common purchasers or 
carriers of natural gas and may amend its rate orders. MCL 483.110. The issue in 
question – whether contingency expenses were just and prudent – is limited in 
scope. A full rate case for such a limited issue would be wasteful of the resources 
of the Commission, DMLC, and the intervenors, while merely addressing this issue 
through an audited report would have the benefit of requiring few resources and 
requiring less time from the parties than a full case. 

Staff’s answer, p. 9. 

Discussion 

Rule 437 provides that a petition for rehearing may be based on a claim of error, newly 
discovered evidence, facts or circumstances arising after the hearing, or unintended consequences 
resulting from compliance with the order. Unless a party can show the decision to be incorrect or 
improper because of errors, newly discovered evidence, facts or circumstances arising after the 
hearing, or unintended consequences, the Commission will not grant rehearing. 

The Commission agrees with North Bay, Riverside, the Attorney General, and the Staff and 
finds that none of the issues raised by DMLC justify rehearing or reconsideration based on the 

4 The Attorney General notes here, as recently stated by the Commission, that “‘a petition for 
rehearing is not a vehicle for seeking forms of relief that were not part of the underlying 
proceeding and for which the record is devoid of support.’” Attorney General’s answer, p. 10, 
n. 24 (quoting March 4, 2021 order in Case No. U-20697, p. 13). 

Page 14 
U-20894 
standards under Rule 437, articulated above.5 The Commission does, however, find it appropriate 
to provide further clarification on the issues concerning timing for construction and contingency 
costs. 

With timing, the Commission confirms DMLC’s understanding and agrees with the Staff that 
the July 27 order authorizes DMLC to begin construction relative to the RCC and NMC pipelines 
once any necessary permits and easements are obtained. Actual conversion of the Wet Header 
Pipeline, from gas gathering to dry gas transmission service, is however distinctly contingent on 
Lambda’s completion of its LGWH pipeline. DMLC’s petition for rehearing, p. 2; Staff’s answer, 
p. 5; July 27 order, p. 38, Ordering Paragraph A; September 9 order. 

The Commission also makes clear, in agreement with DMLC and the Staff, in accordance 
with authority set forth under MCL 483.110,6 and accordant with the Commission’s decision on 
this issue in the July 27 order following the contested case hearing in the matter,7 that DMLC may 
file a completion report in this docket using the same methodology and model used in the case for 
the Staff to audit, and for intervenors to review, any contingency costs for this project that were 
actually incurred by DMLC for justness and prudency. The possibility of a subsequent hearing on 

5 In addition to the approval for the LGWH system in the September 9 order, as noted by the 
parties above, it is the Commission’s belief and understanding that the timing for conversion is 
still on track, consistent with the Commission’s earlier expressed expectations set forth in the 
July 27 order. July 27 order, p. 16. 

6 Notably, in the September 19, 1977 order in Case Nos. U-4968 and U-4982 (September 19 
order), the Commission adopted the findings of fact and conclusions of law of the administrative 
law judge, wherein the administrative law judge in that consolidated case concluded, in relevant 
part, that “‘[p]roceedings initiated in accordance with provisions of MCLA 483.110 to alter or 
amend the price paid by a going common purchaser for natural gas is held pursuant to 
MCLA 460.552 and, hence, the proceedings are not in the nature of rate cases held in compliance 
with MCLA 460.557.’” September 19 order, p. 2. 

7 July 27 order, pp. 26-27. 

Page 15 
U-20894 
this limited issue would then be dependent on this filing from DMLC and any objections thereafter 
following audit and review. 

THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED that the motion for rehearing, reconsideration, and 
clarification filed by DTE Michigan Lateral Company is granted in part and denied in part, as set 
forth in this order. 

The Commission reserves jurisdiction and may issue further orders as necessary. 

Page 16 
U-20894 

Any party desiring to appeal this order must do so in the appropriate court within 30 days after 
issuance and notice of this order, pursuant to MCL 462.26. To comply with the Michigan Rules of 
Court’s requirement to notify the Commission of an appeal, appellants shall send required notices 
to both the Commission’s Executive Secretary and to the Commission’s Legal Counsel. 
Electronic notifications should be sent to the Executive Secretary at mpscedockets@michigan.gov 
and to the Michigan Department of the Attorney General – Public Service Division at 
pungp1@michigan.gov. In lieu of electronic submissions, paper copies of such notifications may 
be sent to the Executive Secretary and the Attorney General – Public Service Division at 7109 
W. Saginaw Hwy., Lansing, MI 48917.
